</table>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In temporal reasoning, <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">Mem0</mtext><mi mathsize="0.710em">g</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}</annotation></semantics></math> substantially outperforms other methods, validating that structured relational graphs excel in capturing chronological relationships and event sequences. The presence of explicit relational context significantly enhances <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">Mem0</mtext><mi mathsize="0.710em">g</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}</annotation></semantics></math>’s temporal coherence, outperforming <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Mem0</span>’s dense memory storage and highlighting the importance of precise relational representations when tracking temporally sensitive information. Open-domain performance further reinforces the value of relational modeling. <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">Mem0</mtext><mi mathsize="0.710em">g</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}</annotation></semantics></math>, benefiting from the relational clarity of graph-based memory, closely competes with the top-performing baseline (Zep). This competitive result underscores <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">Mem0</mtext><mi mathsize="0.710em">g</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}</annotation></semantics></math>’s robustness in integrating external knowledge through relational clarity, suggesting an optimal synergy between structured memory and open-domain information synthesis.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Overall, our analysis indicates complementary strengths of <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Mem0</span> and <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">Mem0</mtext><mi mathsize="0.710em">g</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}</annotation></semantics></math> across various task demands: dense, natural-language-based memory offers significant efficiency for simpler queries, while explicit relational modeling becomes essential for tasks demanding nuanced temporal and contextual integration.
These findings reinforce the importance of adaptable memory structures tailored to specific reasoning contexts in AI agent deployments.</p>
</div>

</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Performance Comparison of <span id="S4.SS3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Mem0</span> and <math id="S4.SS3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">Mem0</mtext><mi mathsize="0.710em">g</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}</annotation></semantics></math> Against RAG Approaches and Full-Context Model</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Comparisons in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Cross-Category Analysis ‣ 4 Evaluation Results, Analysis and Discussion. ‣ Mem0: Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, focusing on the ‘Overall J’ column, reveal that both <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Mem0</span> and <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">Mem0</mtext><mi mathsize="0.710em">g</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}</annotation></semantics></math> consistently outperform all RAG configurations, which vary chunk sizes (128–8192 tokens) and retrieve either one (<math id="S4.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>=1) or two (<math id="S4.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>=2) chunks. Even the strongest RAG approach peaks at around 61% in the J metric, whereas <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Mem0</span> reaches 67%—about a 10% relative improvement—and <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">Mem0</mtext><mi mathsize="0.710em">g</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}</annotation></semantics></math> reaches over 68%, achieving around a 12% relative gain. These advances underscore the advantage of capturing only the most salient facts in memory, rather than retrieving large chunk of original text. By converting the conversation history into concise, structured representations, <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Mem0</span> and <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">Mem0</mtext><mi mathsize="0.710em">g</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}</annotation></semantics></math> mitigate noise and surface more precise cues to the LLM, leading to better answers as evaluated by an external LLM (J).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Despite these improvements, a full-context method that ingests a chunk of roughly 26,000 tokens still achieves the highest J score (approximately 73%). However, as shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F4.sf2" title="Figure 4(b) ‣ Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 Cross-Category Analysis ‣ 4 Evaluation Results, Analysis and Discussion. ‣ Mem0: Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4(b)</span></a>, it also incurs a very high total p95 latency—around 17 seconds—since the model must read the entire conversation on every query. By contrast, <span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Mem0</span> and <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">Mem0</mtext><mi mathsize="0.710em">g</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}</annotation></semantics></math> significantly reduce token usage and thus achieve lower p95 latencies of around 1.44 seconds (a 92% reduction) and 2.6 seconds (a 85% reduction), respectively over full-context approach. Although the full-context approach can provide a slight accuracy edge, the memory-based systems offer a more practical trade-off, maintaining near-competitive quality while imposing only a fraction of the token and latency cost.
As conversation length increases, full-context approaches suffer from exponential growth in computational overhead (evident in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Cross-Category Analysis ‣ 4 Evaluation Results, Analysis and Discussion. ‣ Mem0: Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> where total p95 latency increases significantly with larger <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> values or chunk sizes). This increase in input chunks leads to longer response times and higher token consumption costs. In contrast, memory-focused approaches like <span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Mem0</span> and <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">Mem0</mtext><mi mathsize="0.710em">g</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}</annotation></semantics></math> maintain consistent performance regardless of conversation length, making them substantially more viable for production-scale deployments where efficiency and responsiveness are critical.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Latency Analysis</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Cross-Category Analysis ‣ 4 Evaluation Results, Analysis and Discussion. ‣ Mem0: Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> provides a comprehensive performance comparison of various retrieval and memory methodologies, presenting median (p50) and tail (p95) latencies for both the search phase and total response generation across the <span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">LOCOMO</span> dataset. Our analysis reveals distinct performance patterns governed by architectural choices. Memory-centric architectures demonstrate different performance characteristics. A-Mem, despite its larger memory store, incurs substantial search overhead (p50: 0.668s), resulting in total median latencies of 1.410s. LangMem exhibits even higher search latencies (p50: 17.99s, p95: 59.82s), rendering it impractical for interactive applications. Zep achieves moderate performance (p50 total: 1.292s).
The full-context baseline, which processes the entire conversation history without retrieval, fundamentally differs from retrieval-based approaches. By passing the entire conversation context (26000 tokens) directly to the LLM, it eliminates search overhead but incurs extreme total latencies (p50: 9.870s, p95: 17.117s). Similarly, the OpenAI implementation does not perform memory search, as it processes manually extracted memories from their playground. While this approach achieves impressive response generation times (p50: 0.466s, p95: 0.889s), it requires pre-extraction of relevant context, which is not reflected in the reported metrics.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our proposed <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Mem0</span> approach achieves the lowest search latency among all methods (p50: 0.148s, p95: 0.200s) as illustrated in Figure <a href="#S4.F4.sf1" title="Figure 4(a) ‣ Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 Cross-Category Analysis ‣ 4 Evaluation Results, Analysis and Discussion. ‣ Mem0: Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4(a)</span></a>. This efficiency stems from our selective memory retrieval mechanism and infra improvements that dynamically identifies and retrieves only the most salient information rather than fixed-size chunks. Consequently, <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Mem0</span> maintains the lowest total median latency (0.708s) with remarkably contained p95 values (1.440s), making it particularly suitable for latency-sensitive applications such as interactive AI agents. The graph-enhanced <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">Mem0</mtext><mi mathsize="0.710em">g</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}</annotation></semantics></math> variant introduces additional relational modeling capabilities at a moderate latency cost, with search times (0.476s) still outperforming all existing memory solutions and baselines.
Despite this increase, <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">Mem0</mtext><mi mathsize="0.710em">g</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}</annotation></semantics></math> maintains competitive total latencies (p50: 1.091s, p95: 2.590s) while achieving the highest J score (68.44%) across all methods—trailing only the computationally prohibitive full-context approach.
This performance profile demonstrates our methods’ ability to balance response quality and computational efficiency, offering a compelling solution for production AI agents where both factors are critical constraints.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>Memory System Overhead: Token Analysis and Construction Time</h3>

<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We measure the average token budget required to materialise each system’s long<span id="S4.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">-</span>term memory store.
<span id="S4.SS5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Mem0</span> encodes complete dialogue turns in a natural language representation and therefore occupies only <span id="S4.SS5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">7k</span> tokens per conversation on an average. Where as <math id="S4.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">Mem0</mtext><mi mathsize="0.710em">g</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}</annotation></semantics></math> roughly doubles the footprint to <span id="S4.SS5.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">14k</span> tokens, due to the introduction of graph memories which includes nodes and corresponding relationships. In stark contrast, Zep’s memory graph consumes in excess of <span id="S4.SS5.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">600k</span> tokens. The inflation arises from Zep’s design choice to cache a full abstractive summary at every node while also storing facts on the connecting edges, leading to extensive redundancy across the graph. For perspective, supplying the <em id="S4.SS5.p1.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">entire</em> raw conversation context to the language model—without any memory abstraction—amounts to roughly <span id="S4.SS5.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">26k</span> tokens on average, 20 times less relative to Zep’s graph.
Beyond token inefficiency, our experiments revealed significant operational bottlenecks with Zep. After adding memories to Zep’s system, we observed that immediate memory retrieval attempts often failed to answer our queries correctly. Interestingly, re-running identical searches after a delay of several hours yielded considerably better results. This latency suggests that Zep’s graph construction involves multiple asynchronous LLM calls and extensive background processing, making the memory system impractical for real-time applications. In contrast, <span id="S4.SS5.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Mem0</span> graph construction completes in under a minute even in worst-case scenarios, allowing users to immediately leverage newly added memories for query responses.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">These findings highlight that Zep not only replicates identical knowledge fragments across multiple nodes, but also introduces significant operational delays. Our architectures—<span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Mem0</span> and <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">Mem0</mtext><mi mathsize="0.710em">g</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}</annotation></semantics></math>—preserve the same information at a fraction of the token cost and with substantially faster memory availability, offering a more memory<span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text">-</span>efficient and operationally responsive representation.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion and Future Work</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We have introduced <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Mem0</span> and <math id="S5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">Mem0</mtext><mi mathsize="0.710em">g</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}</annotation></semantics></math>, two complementary memory architectures that overcome the intrinsic limitations of fixed context windows in LLMs. By dynamically extracting, consolidating, and retrieving compact memory representations, <span id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Mem0</span> achieves state-of-the-art performance across single<span id="S5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text">-</span>hop and multi<span id="S5.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text">-</span>hop reasoning, while <math id="S5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">Mem0</mtext><mi mathsize="0.710em">g</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}</annotation></semantics></math>’s graph<span id="S5.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text">-</span>based extensions unlock significant gains in temporal and open<span id="S5.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text">-</span>domain tasks. On the <span id="S5.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">LOCOMO</span> benchmark, our methods deliver 5%, 11%, and 7% relative improvements in single-hop, temporal, and multi-hop reasoning question types over best performing methods in respective question type and reduce p95 latency by over 91% compared to full<span id="S5.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text">-</span>context baselines—demonstrating a powerful balance between precision and responsiveness. <span id="S5.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Mem0</span>’s dense memory pipeline excels at rapid retrieval for straightforward queries, minimizing token usage and computational overhead. In contrast, <math id="S5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">Mem0</mtext><mi mathsize="0.710em">g</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}</annotation></semantics></math>’s structured graph representations provide nuanced relational clarity, enabling complex event sequencing and rich context integration without sacrificing practical efficiency. Together, they form a versatile memory toolkit that adapts to diverse conversational demands while remaining deployable at scale.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Future research directions include optimizing graph operations to reduce the latency overhead in <math id="S5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">Mem0</mtext><mi mathsize="0.710em">g</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}</annotation></semantics></math>, exploring hierarchical memory architectures that blend efficiency with relational representation, and developing more sophisticated memory consolidation mechanisms inspired by human cognitive processes. Additionally, extending our memory frameworks to domains beyond conversational scenarios, such as procedural reasoning and multimodal interactions, would further validate their broader applicability. By addressing the fundamental limitations of fixed context windows, our work represents a significant advancement toward conversational AI systems capable of maintaining coherent, contextually rich interactions over extended periods, much like their human counterparts.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="Ax1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span id="Ax1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_align_center" style="font-size:173%;">Appendix</span></h2>

</section>
<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Prompts</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In developing our LLM-as-a-Judge prompt, we adapt elements from the prompt released by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Packer et al. (2023)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.tab1" class="ltx_float ltx_float_tcbfloat"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="A1.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="380.68" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 700.39 380.68" width="700.39"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,380.68) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#404040;" fill="#404040" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 374.78 C 0 378.04 2.64 380.68 5.91 380.68 L 694.49 380.68 C 697.75 380.68 700.39 378.04 700.39 374.78 L 700.39 5.91 C 700.39 2.64 697.75 0 694.49 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2F2;" fill="#F2F2F2" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 356.57 L 698.43 356.57 L 698.43 5.91 C 698.43 3.73 696.66 1.97 694.49 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 365.17)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:47.49em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;" height="12.3" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="657.13"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="A1.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:47.49em;">
<span id="A1.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">Prompt Template for LLM as a Judge</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 333.14)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:47.49em;--ltx-fo-height:0.84em;--ltx-fo-depth:23.08em;font-size:10pt;" height="330.98" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 11.62)" width="657.13"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="A1.pic1.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:47.49em;">
<span id="A1.pic1.2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Your task is to label an answer to a question as "CORRECT" or "WRONG".
You will be given the following data:
(1) a question (posed by one user to another user),
(2) a ‘gold’ (ground truth) answer,
(3) a generated answer
which you will score as CORRECT/WRONG.
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic1.2.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic1.2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The point of the question is to ask about something one user should know about the other user based on their prior conversations.
The gold answer will usually be a concise and short answer that includes the referenced topic, for example:
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic1.2.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic1.2.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Question: Do you remember what I got the last time I went to Hawaii?
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic1.2.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic1.2.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Gold answer: A shell necklace
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic1.2.5" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic1.2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The generated answer might be much longer, but you should be generous with your grading - as long as it touches on the same topic as the gold answer, it should be counted as CORRECT.
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic1.2.6" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic1.2.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">For time related questions, the gold answer will be a specific date, month, year, etc. The generated answer might be much longer or use relative time references (like ‘last Tuesday’ or ‘next month’), but you should be generous with your grading - as long as it refers to the same date or time period as the gold answer, it should be counted as CORRECT. Even if the format differs (e.g., ‘May 7th’ vs ‘7 May’), consider it CORRECT if it’s the same date.
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic1.2.7" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic1.2.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Now it’s time for the real question:
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic1.2.8" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic1.2.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Question: {question}
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic1.2.9" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic1.2.9.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Gold answer: {gold_answer}
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic1.2.10" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic1.2.10.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Generated answer: {generated_answer}
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic1.2.11" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic1.2.11.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">First, provide a short (one sentence) explanation of your reasoning, then finish with CORRECT or WRONG.
Do NOT include both CORRECT and WRONG in your response, or it will break the evaluation script.
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic1.2.12" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic1.2.12.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Just return the label CORRECT or WRONG in a json format with the key as "label".
</span><span id="A1.pic1.2.12.2" class="ltx_text"></span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</figure>
<figure id="A1.tab2" class="ltx_float ltx_float_tcbfloat"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="A1.pic2" class="ltx_picture" height="560.74" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 700.39 560.74" width="700.39"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,560.74) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#404040;" fill="#404040" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 554.84 C 0 558.1 2.64 560.74 5.91 560.74 L 694.49 560.74 C 697.75 560.74 700.39 558.1 700.39 554.84 L 700.39 5.91 C 700.39 2.64 697.75 0 694.49 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2F2;" fill="#F2F2F2" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 519.26 L 698.43 519.26 L 698.43 5.91 C 698.43 3.73 696.66 1.97 694.49 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 545.23)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:47.49em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:1.45em;font-size:10pt;" height="29.67" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="657.13"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="A1.pic2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:47.49em;">
<span id="A1.pic2.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">Prompt Template for Results Generation (<span id="A1.pic2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Mem0</span>)</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 483.83)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:47.49em;--ltx-fo-height:1.71em;--ltx-fo-depth:33.97em;font-size:10pt;" height="493.68" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 23.62)" width="657.13"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="A1.pic2.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:47.49em;">
<span id="A1.pic2.2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic2.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">You are an intelligent memory assistant tasked with retrieving accurate information from conversation memories. </span></span>
<span id="A1.pic2.2.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic2.2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"># CONTEXT: </span></span>
<span id="A1.pic2.2.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic2.2.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">You have access to memories from two speakers in a conversation. These memories contain timestamped information that may be relevant to answering the question.
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic2.2.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic2.2.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"># INSTRUCTIONS: </span></span>
<span id="A1.pic2.2.5" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic2.2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">1. Carefully analyze all provided memories from both speakers
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic2.2.6" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic2.2.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">2. Pay special attention to the timestamps to determine the answer
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic2.2.7" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic2.2.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">3. If the question asks about a specific event or fact, look for direct evidence in the memories
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic2.2.8" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic2.2.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">4. If the memories contain contradictory information, prioritize the most recent memory
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic2.2.9" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic2.2.9.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">5. If there is a question about time references (like "last year", "two months ago", etc.),
calculate the actual date based on the memory timestamp. For example, if a memory from
4 May 2022 mentions "went to India last year," then the trip occurred in 2021.
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic2.2.10" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic2.2.10.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">6. Always convert relative time references to specific dates, months, or years. For example,
convert "last year" to "2022" or "two months ago" to "March 2023" based on the memory
timestamp. Ignore the reference while answering the question.
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic2.2.11" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic2.2.11.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">7. Focus only on the content of the memories from both speakers. Do not confuse character
names mentioned in memories with the actual users who created those memories.
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic2.2.12" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic2.2.12.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">8. The answer should be less than 5-6 words.
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic2.2.13" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic2.2.13.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"># APPROACH (Think step by step): </span></span>
<span id="A1.pic2.2.14" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic2.2.14.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">1. First, examine all memories that contain information related to the question
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic2.2.15" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic2.2.15.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">2. Examine the timestamps and content of these memories carefully
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic2.2.16" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic2.2.16.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">3. Look for explicit mentions of dates, times, locations, or events that answer the question
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic2.2.17" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic2.2.17.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">4. If the answer requires calculation (e.g., converting relative time references), show your work
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic2.2.18" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic2.2.18.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">5. Formulate a precise, concise answer based solely on the evidence in the memories
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic2.2.19" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic2.2.19.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">6. Double-check that your answer directly addresses the question asked
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic2.2.20" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic2.2.20.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">7. Ensure your final answer is specific and avoids vague time references
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic2.2.21" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic2.2.21.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Memories for user {speaker_1_user_id}:
</span></span>

<span id="A1.pic3.2.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic3.2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"># APPROACH (Think step by step):</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic3.2.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic3.2.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">1. First, examine all memories that contain information related to the question
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic3.2.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic3.2.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">2. Examine the timestamps and content of these memories carefully
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic3.2.5" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic3.2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">3. Look for explicit mentions of dates, times, locations, or events that answer the
question
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic3.2.6" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic3.2.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">4. If the answer requires calculation (e.g., converting relative time references),
show your work
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic3.2.7" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic3.2.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">5. Analyze the knowledge graph relations to understand the user’s knowledge context
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic3.2.8" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic3.2.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">6. Formulate a precise, concise answer based solely on the evidence in the memories
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic3.2.9" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic3.2.9.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">7. Double-check that your answer directly addresses the question asked
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic3.2.10" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic3.2.10.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">8. Ensure your final answer is specific and avoids vague time references
</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic3.2.11" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic3.2.11.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Memories for user {speaker_1_user_id}:

</span></span>
<span id="A1.pic3.2.13" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.pic3.2.13.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Relations for user {speaker_1_user_id}:

<div id="alg1.l1" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">1:</span></span>
            
            
          <span id="alg1.l1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Input:</span> Set of retrieved memories <math id="alg1.l1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>F</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F</annotation></semantics></math>, Existing memory store <math id="alg1.l1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=\{m_{1},m_{2},\ldots,m_{n}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=\{m_{1},m_{2},\ldots,m_{n}\}</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l2" class="ltx_listingline">

          <span id="alg1.l2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Output:</span> Updated memory store <math id="alg1.l2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math>
<span class="ltx_rule" style="width:100%;height:1px;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span>

<div id="alg1.l3" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">3:</span></span>
            
            
          <span id="alg1.l3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">procedure</span> <span id="alg1.l3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">UpdateMemory</span>(<math id="alg1.l3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F,M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F,M</annotation></semantics></math>)

</div>
<div id="alg1.l4" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">4:</span></span>
            
            
            <span id="alg1.l4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span> each fact <math id="alg1.l4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f\in F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>F</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f\in F</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="alg1.l4.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">do</span>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l5" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">5:</span></span>
            
            
             <math id="alg1.l5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="operation\leftarrow\textsc{ClassifyOperation}(f,M)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">ClassifyOperation</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">operation\leftarrow\textsc{ClassifyOperation}(f,M)</annotation></semantics></math>
<span id="alg1.l5.3" class="ltx_text" style="float:right;"><math id="alg1.l5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\triangleright" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⊳</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\triangleright</annotation></semantics></math> Execute appropriate operation based on classification
</span>
</div>
<div id="alg1.l6" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">6:</span></span>
            
            
             <span id="alg1.l6.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">if</span> <math id="alg1.l6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="operation=\text{ADD}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mtext>ADD</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">operation=\text{ADD}</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="alg1.l6.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">then</span>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l7" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l7.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">7:</span></span>
            
            
               <math id="alg1.l7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="id\leftarrow\text{GenerateUniqueID}()" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mtext>GenerateUniqueID</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">id\leftarrow\text{GenerateUniqueID}()</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l8" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l8.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">8:</span></span>
            
            
               <math id="alg1.l8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext='M\leftarrow M\cup\{(id,f,\text{"ADD"})\}' display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>∪</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>f</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>"ADD"</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\leftarrow M\cup\{(id,f,\text{"ADD"})\}</annotation></semantics></math>
<span id="alg1.l8.3" class="ltx_text" style="float:right;"><math id="alg1.l8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\triangleright" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⊳</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\triangleright</annotation></semantics></math> Add new fact with unique identifier
</span>
</div>
<div id="alg1.l9" class="ltx_listingline">

<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Selected Baselines</h2>

<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">LoCoMo</h4>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The LoCoMo framework implements a sophisticated memory pipeline that enables LLM agents to maintain coherent, long-term conversations. At its core, the system divides memory into short-term and long-term components. After each conversation session, agents generate summaries (stored as short-term memory) that distill key information from that interaction. Simultaneously, individual conversation turns are transformed into ‘<span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">observations</span>’ - factual statements about each speaker’s persona and life events that are stored in long-term memory with references to the specific dialog turns that produced them. When generating new responses, agents leverage both the most recent session summary and selectively retrieve relevant observations from their long-term memory. This dual-memory approach is further enhanced by incorporating a temporal event graph that tracks causally connected life events occurring between conversation sessions. By conditioning responses on retrieved memories, current conversation context, persona information, and intervening life events, the system enables agents to maintain consistent personalities and recall important details across conversations spanning hundreds of turns and dozens of sessions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">ReadAgent</h4>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">ReadAgent addresses the fundamental limitations of LLMs by emulating how humans process lengthy texts through a sophisticated three-stage pipeline. First, in Episode Pagination, the system intelligently segments text at natural cognitive boundaries rather than arbitrary cutoffs. Next, during Memory Gisting, it distills each segment into concise summaries that preserve essential meaning while drastically reducing token count—similar to how human memory retains the substance of information without verbatim recall. Finally, when tasked with answering questions, the Interactive Lookup mechanism examines these gists and strategically retrieves only the most relevant original text segments for detailed processing. This human-inspired approach enables LLMs to effectively manage documents up to 20 times longer than their normal context windows. By balancing global understanding through gists with selective attention to details, ReadAgent achieves both computational efficiency and improved comprehension, demonstrating that mimicking human cognitive processes can significantly enhance AI text processing capabilities.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">MemoryBank</h4>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The MemoryBank system enhances LLMs with long-term memory through a sophisticated three-part pipeline. At its core, the Memory Storage component warehouses detailed conversation logs, hierarchical event summaries, and evolving user personality profiles. When a new interaction occurs, the Memory Retrieval mechanism employs a dual-tower dense retrieval model to extract contextually relevant past information. The Memory Updating component, provides a human-like forgetting mechanism where memories strengthen when recalled and naturally decay over time if unused. This comprehensive approach enables AI companions to recall pertinent information, maintain contextual awareness across extended interactions, and develop increasingly accurate user portraits, resulting in more personalized and natural long-term conversations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">MemGPT</h4>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The MemGPT system introduces an operating system-inspired approach to overcome the context window limitations inherent in LLMs. At its core, MemGPT employs a sophisticated memory management pipeline consisting of three key components: a hierarchical memory system, self-directed memory operations, and an event-based control flow mechanism. The system divides available memory into ‘<span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">main context</span>’ (analogous to RAM in traditional operating systems) and ‘<span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">external context</span>’ (analogous to disk storage). The main context—which is bound by the LLM’s context window—contains system instructions, recent conversation history, and working memory that can be modified by the model. The external context stores unlimited information outside the model’s immediate context window, including complete conversation histories and archival data. When the LLM needs information not present in main context, it can initiate function calls to search, retrieve, or modify content across these memory tiers, effectively ‘<span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">paging</span>’ relevant information in and out of its limited context window. This OS-inspired architecture enables MemGPT to maintain conversational coherence over extended interactions, manage documents that exceed standard context limits, and perform multi-hop information retrieval tasks—all while operating with fixed-context models. The system’s ability to intelligently manage its own memory resources provides the illusion of infinite context, significantly extending what’s possible with current LLM technology.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">A-Mem</h4>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The A-Mem model introduces an agentic memory system designed for LLM agents. This system dynamically structures and evolves memories through interconnected notes. Each note captures interactions enriched with structured attributes like keywords, contextual descriptions, and tags generated by the LLM. Upon creating a new memory, A-MEM uses semantic embeddings to retrieve relevant existing notes, then employs an LLM-driven approach to establish meaningful links based on similarities and shared attributes. Crucially, the memory evolution mechanism updates existing notes dynamically, refining their contextual information and attributes whenever new relevant memories are integrated. Thus, memory structure continually evolves, allowing richer and contextually deeper connections among memories. Retrieval from memory is conducted through semantic similarity, providing relevant historical context during agent interactions</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</article>
</div>
</div>
